newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK manufacturing grows for 14th month in row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK manufacturing grows for 14th month in row.

text.p: Britain's manufacturing sector grew for the fourteenth month in succession in July despite a sharp fall in export demand, according to a leading business survey published on Friday.
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said its purchasing managers' index (PMI) slipped slightly to 53.4 from 53.5 in June, but any reading over 50 represents expansion.

The PMI survey, sponsored by Reuters, is likely to reinforce the Bank of England's concerns about the strength of domestic demand. Economists said it increased the chances of a rise in Britain's 6.75 percent interest rates at next week's meeting of the central bank's monetary policy committee.
The survey showed output was holding up well despite the dampening impact of the strong pound on demand for British exports.
"The continued expansion of the manufacturing economy largely reflected a strong rise in output during the month," CIPS said.
Order books strengthened for the 14th consecutive month with consumer-driven domestic demand once more the principal source of new business.
"The pace of growth slowed slightly, however, as export orders fell for the first time since this survey began monitoring exports in January 1996."
The decline was almost entirely attributed to the rise in the value of the pound reducing the competitiveness of British goods overseas.

Analysts said the survey showed a clear weakening of export orders. "Prospects for exports are showing signs of steady deterioration. The odd thing is that it hasn't come through in the trade figures yet," said Philip Shaw, economist at Investec Bank.
But the strong pound offered some good news on the inflation front, continuing to reduce the cost of imported goods for manufacturers.

Average costs of fuel and raw materials purchased by manufacturing firms recorded the sharpest monthly fall since the survey began in July 1991, with almost one in three firms reporting a reduction in average prices compared to the previous month.
Employment rose for the 13th month in a row, but growth was more muted than in previous months as an increasing number of firms laid off employees because of weakened export order books.

And, despite eagerness among purchasing managers to buy as few goods as necessary in order to reduce costs, the July survey found a further deterioration in suppliers' delivery times, reflecting growing capacity constraints and supply bottlenecks.
